rejectedInVerify.title: X-ray diffraction: reading a crystal
rejectedInVerify.reason: It duplicates another candidate in this pool: physics.json's crystal-diffraction (L3) has the same mechanism and takeaway (build or load a cell, structure factors make reflections appear or vanish, rotate the crystal through the beam, compute a COD powder pattern; 'the brightness of each spot encodes where the atoms sit'). Only one of the two should survive. Otherwise it is sound: COD data are CC0 / public domain, scattering factors are available through BSD-licensed xraylib, and the level is honest (MIT 3.091). It can't stand as a separate topic; merge it into crystal-diffraction, adding its wavelength control and Ewald sphere there, or drop crystal-diffraction in its favour.

gapSwaps.inTitle: Camouflage: you are the hungry bird

criticNotes.missing: I looked for core degree models that no existing, proposed or runner-up topic covers. Math: linear programming and the simplex method, numerical root-finding (Newton's method and its basins), least-squares regression and the SVD, and numerical ODE stability (Euler against Runge-Kutta, stiffness). All of these are strong, but they overlap partly with gradient-descent, dimensionality-reduction, how-simulations-work and differential-equations, so I did not propose them. Linear programming is the best remaining math candidate. Chemistry: IR spectroscopy from the normal modes of a small molecule. It is a good level-3 candidate, but it sits close to the nmr and mass-spectrometry runners-up, and real spectra would need NIST data whose licence is not fully open. Biology: phylogenetic tree building (neighbour-joining or UPGMA) would pair with sequence-alignment, and Hodgkin-Huxley is already largely covered by neurons plus membrane-potential. Medicine: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (close to clinical-trials), the Windkessel model of arterial pressure (close to heart-circulation) and the respiratory mechanics of a ventilator are all still open. Earth: geostrophic balance and Rossby waves are partly in atmosphere-weather, and seismic ray tracing and earthquake location are partly in earthquakes. Isostasy and lithospheric flexure is a clean level-3 gap. Networks: distance-vector routing (Bellman-Ford and count-to-infinity) partly overlaps internet and graph-search, and Shannon channel capacity is partly in error-correction and wireless-signals. Energy: heat exchangers (NTU method) and thermal conduction in fins are core mechanical engineering gaps not chosen here. I found no openly licensed real-data gaps among these: each of the six proposals runs on a self-contained model, with optional open data (UniProt CC BY 4.0, BLOSUM62 public domain, SRTM public domain, IUPHAR CC BY-SA 4.0). On the user's AI tilt: these six deliberately fill non-AI degree cores, and the AI ladder is already dense in the proposal.

I checked the existing 100 and the proposed and runner-up lists against the NGSS grades 3-8 and KS2/KS3 core, and against the questions children ask most. Six gaps were clear: the water cycle (KS2 Year 4, and the catalogue says it isn't covered), erosion and deposition by rivers (NGSS 4-ESS2-1, the stream-table lab), why the Moon doesn't fall (KS2 Year 5 gravity), friction (KS2 Year 5), camouflage and adaptation with the reader as predator (KS2 Year 6), and a level-0 reinforcement-learning page, which follows the user's preference for AI. Everything I looked at but didn't propose:

Already covered, or too close to an existing page:
- Day and night, seasons and moon phases: in sun-earth-moon.
- Simple circuits with a switch and a bulb: electric-circuits, plus light-bulb-hot-wire in the runners-up.
- Thermal insulators, such as why a flask keeps tea warm: close to why-metal-feels-cold.
- Teeth and digestion: enzymes-and-digestion.
- Heartbeat during exercise: heart-circulation.
- Germs and handwashing: epidemics.
- Food chains and food webs: ecosystems L1 already has a remove-a-species food web. A level-0 version would only re-skin it.
- Pollination by bees, and seed dispersal: real curriculum, but no clear model whose takeaway shows in the graphic. Weak.
- Decomposers and compost (NGSS 5-LS2-1): no honest interactive model I could find.
- How plants drink water (KS2 Year 3, the celery experiment): the transpiration model would be contrived.
- Scale of the solar system (NGSS 5-ESS1-1): just a zoomable diagram, which the rules exclude.
- Stars wheeling around the pole star (NGSS 5-ESS1-2): possible with the HYG star catalogue (CC BY-SA), but it's close to sun-earth-moon. Held back.
- Why bubbles are round (surface tension): real ELI5 demand, but no curriculum anchor. Held back.
- Programming a robot with sequence, loops and debugging (KS2 computing core): a strong runner-up, close to solving-a-maze and sorting-network. I chose the AI candidate instead, following the user's preference.

Not found anywhere in the three lists: rock types and the rock cycle at level 0 (deep-time and plate-tectonics only touch it), and mixtures with filtering and sieving. Both are thin as models.

Of the six, only be-the-bird-camouflage needs outside artwork (CC0 bark photos or procedural textures), and friction-slide-or-stick needs a CC BY friction table (OpenStax). The other four need no data.

I checked famous 'how does X work' subjects against both lists using Google question lists, NOAA and NWS lightning pages, the PhET list, 3Blue1Brown's deep-learning series, Anthropic's interpretability papers (induction heads, toy models of superposition) and RAG primers. The six entries fill three gaps. Two are LLM internals: how a model copies from its prompt (induction heads) and how it stores more features than it has neurons (superposition). The third is a common chatbot question: how it looks things up (RAG). Together they fill out the LLM ladder from tokenization to serving. There are also three everyday classics: the microwave oven, lightning, and static electricity on a balloon (one of PhET's most used simulations). Considered but not proposed: (1) Capacitive touchscreens: a strong everyday subject with a real model (a grid of crossing capacitors, a finger lowering readings, the centroid giving the position, which also explains multi-touch and gloves). It was cut only to stay within six, and it is the first runner-up. (2) Hurricanes: already grown inside atmosphere-weather. (3) Noise cancelling and the refrigerator: already runners-up. (4) LLM 'hallucination': much asked about, but there is no honest small model separate from language-models and rlhf-alignment. (5) Sparse autoencoders and interpretability features: could be a later step of superposition-toy-models rather than a separate page. (6) Grokking: modular addition trained in the browser is feasible, but it is a niche next to induction heads. (7) CLIP and image-text models: no small, openly licensed paired dataset that runs in the browser. (8) Tool use and agents: no honest model that fits in a page. (9) Sampling and temperature: already in language-models. (10) Induction hobs, LEDs, SSD and flash memory, contactless and NFC payments, memory and sleep in the brain, nuclear weapons: in turn too close to motors-generators, semiconductors and transistors, wireless-signals, why-you-get-sleepy, or nuclear-fission, or not suited to the site. Google publishes no current ranking of 'how does' science questions, so demand here rests on explainer channels, PhET and agency pages rather than search volumes.

runnersUp.title: Milk, vinegar and yogurt
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Charged protein balls clumping when acid is added or made by bacteria is a clear mechanism that ties curds and yogurt together without a pH number, distinct from acids-bases.

build 4: Brownian colloids whose repulsion switches off as pH falls, plus a temperature-dependent bacterial acidification rate, can be built at interactive rates and show curdling emerging. The thicker set from preheated milk would need an extra stated rule (denatured whey binding the casein).
runnersUp.verifyNote: Distinct from acids-bases and from the pool's cooking-an-egg (proteins unfolding in heat), and buildable: Brownian colloid particles whose repulsion falls as pH nears casein's isoelectric point (about 4.6), plus bacterial growth with a temperature optimum that makes the acid. The pitfall is wrong in two ways. Most cheese is set by rennet, an enzyme that clips kappa-casein, not by acid, so 'the same clumping is cheese' is false except for acid cheeses such as paneer or ricotta. And raw milk turns sour through lactic acid bacteria much like yogurt cultures, which contradicts 'the bacteria in yogurt are not the bacteria that spoil food'. 'Kept apart by their charge' also oversimplifies: the micelles are held apart by a charged, hairy kappa-casein coat, mostly by its bulk. needsSource should name the few constants it uses.

fix.takeaway: Milk is a cloud of tiny protein balls kept apart by a charged, fuzzy coat; acid, poured in or made by bacteria, takes the charge away and lets them clump, which is curds in a minute or yogurt overnight.
fix.pitfall: Curdling milk with vinegar is not milk 'going off', though milk left out does sour the same way, by lactic acid bacteria much like yogurt's. Most cheese is not made this way: rennet, an enzyme, sets it by clipping the protein balls' coat, and only some cheeses (paneer, ricotta) are set by acid.
fix.needsSource: No dataset. The model uses textbook constants: casein's isoelectric point near pH 4.6 (dairy-science reviews such as de Kruif's), and yogurt cultures (Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactobacillus bulgaricus) that work best around 40 to 45 C and stop near fridge temperature. Shown as comparisons, never as numbers.

runnersUp.title: Monte Carlo tree search & AlphaGo
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A playable, clearly mechanistic algorithm (select, expand, rollout, backup) with the AlphaGo upgrade, distinct from graph-search and grid-world RL, and honest at level 3.

build 5: MCTS on Connect Four is a small exact algorithm running thousands of simulations per second client-side, and a self-play policy/value net small enough to ship (own weights) is a standard, modest offline job.

runnersUp.title: The tennis racket theorem: why a spinning handle flips
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A famous, surprising mechanism (Dzhanibekov flip) with the real model (Euler's equations, the angular-momentum sphere) that no existing page touches, and honestly university rigid-body mechanics.

build 5: Euler's rigid-body equations are three ODEs, integrated at interactive rates. The angular-momentum sphere with its energy curves is an exact geometric construction, and the flipping can be seen without reading anything.

runnersUp.title: The Schrödinger equation & the hydrogen atom
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A must-have: shooting the radial equation to its 1/n² levels and checking them against NIST lines is the real model, and it explains what atoms-periodic-table only shows.
build 5: A Numerov shooting solver for the radial equation runs instantly, orbitals come from analytic wavefunctions, and the NIST ASD hydrogen lines are US government data, freely usable.

runnersUp.title: Sink or float
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Density as comparison against the same-size lump of water, with the clay boat and the egg in salt water, is a must-have level-0 mechanism no existing page covers; it arguably belongs in physics.
build 5: Archimedes' equilibrium depth from a dozen published densities, with salt changing the water's density, is an exact, tiny, honest model, and the outcome can be seen directly.

runnersUp.title: Entanglement & Bell's theorem
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A university-level real model (CHSH against any hidden-variable table, with the Delft data) that the graphic can run, clearly beyond quantum-computing's entanglement step.

build 5: A Monte Carlo of reader-defined hidden-variable tables against quantum sampling of the singlet correlations is exact, tiny and honest. The Delft result (S = 2.42 +/- 0.20) can be quoted from the paper, so the 4TU dataset with its non-CC terms is optional and not a blocker.

runnersUp.title: Blackbody radiation from counting modes
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Deriving the Planck curve by counting modes, showing the ultraviolet catastrophe and fitting COBE is a real level-3 mechanism and a clear step beyond stars' use of the curve.

build 5: Counting integer mode triples in a box per frequency band, then weighting by kT or Planck's average, is a real and cheap computation. The FIRAS monopole spectrum is a 2 KB public-domain NASA LAMBDA file.

runnersUp.title: Fluid flow & the Navier-Stokes equations
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A Reynolds-number sweep from creeping flow to a vortex street to turbulence is a visual, famous mechanism, well beyond flight's wing section.

build 4: A D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann solver past a cylinder runs interactively in the browser (Schroeder's demo is the precedent) and produces the eddies and the vortex street; the 'turbulent' end is only 2D and should be labelled that way.

runnersUp.title: The principle of least action
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Dragging a path and watching the action become stationary is an excellent interactive mechanism, foundational at university level and distinct from newtons-laws.

build 4: A discretised path whose action is evaluated live and relaxed by gradient descent is small and honest; the planet case is a saddle rather than a minimum, so 'snaps toward' must find a stationary point, not minimise.

runnersUp.title: Waves at the beach
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A familiar beach, one control (the slope of the sea floor), the bobbing duck and waves breaking in the shallows make an ideal level-0 mechanism that leads naturally into waves-interference.

build 4: Linear dispersion with depth, Green's-law shoaling, a breaking criterion (H/d about 0.78) and orbital particle motion make a cheap, honest kinematic model that is a pure function of time. Breaking itself is a threshold, not simulated.

runnersUp.title: The nephron: filter, then reclaim
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The countercurrent multiplier stepped cycle by cycle is a classic hard-to-picture mechanism that an animation explains well, it is absent from the site, and two other candidates in the batch depend on it.

build 4: The countercurrent multiplier stepped single effect by single effect is a classic, honest algorithm, and ADH-controlled water permeability in the collecting duct is a simple flux model. Filtration and proximal reabsorption are mostly fixed fractions.

runnersUp.title: Dimensionality reduction: PCA & t-SNE
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: PCA as the rotation that keeps the most spread, contrasted with t-SNE's artefacts, covers the other half of the reserve topic and answers embeddings' own pitfall; level 3 is honest for t-SNE.

build 5: PCA on a rotatable 3-D cloud and live t-SNE on a few hundred Fashion-MNIST points (MIT) both run comfortably at interactive rates, and the perplexity and seed artefacts are real outputs of the algorithm.

runnersUp.title: Support vector machines & kernels
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A classic level-3 ML mechanism (maximum margin, support vectors, the kernel trick) with draggable points, distinct from neural-network boundaries.

build 5: A perceptron and an SMO-solved soft-margin SVM with polynomial and RBF kernels on dozens of dragged points solve in milliseconds, so the boundary and support vectors update live as an exact model.

runnersUp.title: Momentum, Adam & learning-rate schedules
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Using conditioning as the control and showing per-parameter scaling and schedules goes properly beyond gradient-descent's momentum toggle, and it is standard university ML.
build 5: SGD, momentum, RMSProp and Adam on a quadratic with adjustable conditioning are a few lines each and run instantly. The small-network loss curve can be trained live, and no data is needed.

runnersUp.title: Evolutionary algorithms
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Gradient-free search with CMA-ES's adapting ellipse and a GA's diversity collapse is a visual mechanism distinct from both evolution (biology) and gradient-descent, and fits level 3.

build 5: CMA-ES on 2-D landscapes and a GA on a small tour are both small exact algorithms, and the stretching covariance ellipse is the algorithm's own state. These are two demos, though, so the page may need to choose one focus.

runnersUp.title: Graph neural networks
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Message passing on the karate club, with oversmoothing and an expressiveness limit, is real level-3 content and goes beyond pagerank's scalar propagation.

build 5: A GCN on the 34-node karate club trains in milliseconds, oversmoothing and the WL-indistinguishable pair come straight from the computation, and the graph is a tiny published fact table that is safe to re-enter with a citation.

runnersUp.title: Decision trees, random forests & gradient boosting
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Greedy splits, bagging and boosting are core ML mechanisms the catalogue lacks, are shown well on the plane, and are distinct from learning-from-data's polynomial fit; three methods make the page long.
build 5: CART splits, bagging and gradient boosting on 2-D points or Palmer penguins (CC0) are exact, fast algorithms rendered as region maps, so every step is a real computation.

runnersUp.title: Quantization: shrinking a model's numbers
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Weights snapping to a coarser grid as the bits drop, with outliers deciding the damage, is a visual and real mechanism; it is distinct from binary and practically important for LLMs.

build 5: One GPT-2 small weight matrix (modified MIT, about 1 MB as fp16) quantized live, plus an offline perplexity sweep and the page's own tiny model, makes a small, honest and fully observable model.

runnersUp.title: Mixture of experts
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A topical level-3 mechanism (routing, load-balancing collapse, parameters stored vs used) distinct from transformers' attention, with a toy 2-D version the graphic can show.

build 5: A router plus a handful of tiny MLP experts on a 2-D regression trains live in milliseconds per step, and collapse without the load-balancing loss is a real, reproducible outcome; no data needed.

runnersUp.title: Gaussian processes
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Clicking in observations and watching the uncertainty band pinch and swell is a direct visual of the real model, it is a core university topic, and it is distinct from every existing page.
build 5: GP regression with a handful of points is a small Cholesky solve, so the posterior band, the sampled functions, kernel swaps and UCB queries are all exact and instant, and no data is needed.

runnersUp.title: Bias, variance & double descent
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: It extends learning-from-data's test-error curve through the interpolation peak with a real random-features model and a bias-variance decomposition, which is clearly level 3 and distinct.

build 5: Random-feature ridge regression is a closed-form linear solve with a few hundred features at most, so sweeping width, resampling and regularisation all compute live, and the interpolation peak emerges from the real model.

runnersUp.title: Operating systems: processes & scheduling
judgeNotes: build 5: FCFS, SJF, round robin and MLFQ over a handful of jobs are tiny discrete-event simulations, and the Gantt chart and metrics follow directly from them.
fit-level 4: Promotes 'Operating systems' from the reserve list: real scheduling policies with Gantt charts and turnaround metrics, distinct from cpu, which runs a single program.

runnersUp.title: How a 3D printer builds a shape
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A familiar machine with a visible mechanism (slicing into layers), one control (layer thickness) and a clean takeaway that a 10-year-old can grasp; it is distinct from graphics-3d.
build 5: Plane-mesh slicing into contours, zigzag infill and overhang detection on a page-generated mesh is a real small algorithm that needs no data.

runnersUp.title: Synchronization: metronomes, bridges and the Kuramoto model
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Sudden synchrony above a coupling threshold is a striking mechanism with real cases (metronomes, the Millennium Bridge), distinct from oscillations-resonance and properly paired with the level-0 fireflies toy.

build 5: A hundred coupled phase ODEs are trivial to run, the order parameter is directly visible, and the Millennium Bridge parameters are published numbers from Strogatz et al. 2005, not data that needs a licence.

runnersUp.title: Bézier curves: how fonts and vector drawings bend
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Repeated straight-line interpolation (de Casteljau) is a real algorithm behind fonts and vector drawing, it draws as a mechanism directly, it is honest at level 1 and no existing page shows it.
build 5: De Casteljau's algorithm with draggable control points, a t scrubber, convex hull and joined segments is the exact model and runs instantly in SVG.

runnersUp.title: Falling & parachutes
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Air on or off for the hammer and feather, and a parachute reaching a steady falling speed, make a clear level-0 mechanism; it is distinct enough from the air-resistance slider on newtons-laws.
build 5: Weight against quadratic drag integrated in time, with an air-off switch, is the textbook honest ODE, and terminal speed and the hammer and feather landing together are directly visible.

runnersUp.title: What a camera's sensor counts
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Light as counted specks in buckets explains grain, overexposure and the colour filter grid with a real mechanism; distinct from light-optics and vision-color.

build 5: Poisson photon counts per photosite, a Bayer mosaic and a neighbour-averaging demosaic on a small grid (a few thousand cells) are an honest model of the real thing, and a CC0 Commons photo is easy to find.

runnersUp.title: Bifurcations & nonlinear dynamics
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Genuine level-3 nonlinear-dynamics content (saddle-node, pitchfork, Hopf) with an animated vector field, distinct from chaos-fractals; it risks becoming a catalogue of types, so it needs one guiding example.

build 5: The normal-form ODEs, animated vector fields and a continuation diagram are trivially interactive. The real-system examples (laser rate equations, a buckling beam, FitzHugh-Nagumo) are each small ODEs.

runnersUp.title: Colliding galaxies
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The Toomre restricted N-body model is visually striking and has a clear tidal mechanism (prograde against retrograde), and no existing page has it; it could almost sit at level 2.
build 5: The Toomre restricted N-body model (two point masses with thousands of test stars) is the classic small, honest model and runs easily in the browser with no data.

runnersUp.title: Oxygen & haemoglobin
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The cooperative binding curve and its shifts (Bohr effect, carbon monoxide) are a core mechanism, distinct from respiration-atp, and a needed prerequisite for lung-gas-exchange and fetal-circulation.
build 5: The Adair or MWC four-site binding curve, the published Bohr, temperature and 2,3-BPG shifts, and the CO competition (Haldane) are closed-form; this is a small, exact model.

runnersUp.title: Luria-Delbruck: mutations before selection
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A landmark experiment run as a clone-statistics simulation whose jackpot distribution shows its own takeaway, and it deepens evolution's pitfall rather than repeating it.

build 5: Growing twenty cultures by branching with mutations at division, against a Poisson alternative, is a trivial simulation, and the jackpot plates and the estimate from the share of empty plates come directly out of it.

runnersUp.title: Pipelines & branch prediction
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Pipeline hazards, forwarding and a two-bit predictor, shown cycle by cycle, are standard computer architecture with a clear diagram, and it is distinct from cpu's one-at-a-time cycle and from the cache candidate.
build 5: A cycle-accurate five-stage pipeline simulator with hazards, forwarding and a two-bit branch predictor is small and exact, and stall and flush counts come from the model.

runnersUp.title: Membrane transport & the resting potential
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A real university mechanism (Nernst/GHK, pump, osmotic volume) that neurons takes for granted, so it is distinct and well suited to a live voltage graphic.
build 5: A pump-leak ODE (ion fluxes by GHK, Na/K pump, osmotic volume) is a few coupled equations that run instantly, and the Nernst and GHK values are exact checks; no data needed.

runnersUp.title: Cell cycle control
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The real Novak-Tyson model at an honest level 3 with a clear takeaway, but its bistable-switch-with-hysteresis lesson repeats lac-operon, epigenetic-memory and genetic-circuits in this same file, so only some of them should be chosen.

build 5: The Tyson or Novak-Tyson ODEs are small, curated in BioModels under CC0, and integrate in real time; the hysteresis loop, the period that changes with growth rate and the checkpoint are all parameters of the real model.

runnersUp.title: The partition function
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Filling energy levels with Boltzmann weights to get the Schottky bump and the freezing-out of heat capacity (checked against diamond) is the real model and distinct from entropy's microstate counting.
build 5: Boltzmann sums over a few level schemes are exact and instant, and Weber's diamond heat-capacity values as tabulated by Einstein in 1907 are public domain.

runnersUp.title: The fast Fourier transform
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The butterfly recursion and the operation count are exactly what a university student learns, and the page is properly distinct from fourier-transform's meaning-of-the-transform page, though it could sit in math rather than computing.
build 5: A radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT on 8 to 64 samples with a drawn butterfly, counted multiplications and FFT polynomial multiplication is exact and trivially fast.

runnersUp.title: Molecular motors: how kinesin walks
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Stochastic stepping, stall force and force-velocity curves are a vivid mechanism the graphic can show, clearly distinct from the ATP synthase rotor in respiration-atp.

build 5: A Gillespie simulation of a discrete-state kinesin model with Fisher-Kolomeisky rates gives the staircase traces and force-velocity curves cheaply, with the parameters taken from the published paper.

runnersUp.title: Cell signalling: cascades & ultrasensitivity
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Huang-Ferrell MAPK ultrasensitivity is a real model with a striking dose-response result, and it is distinct from the hormone-level homeostasis page.
build 5: The Huang-Ferrell MAPK ODEs (BIOMD0000000009, CC0) are a few dozen mass-action equations, and the dose-response steepening is directly computable.

runnersUp.title: Circadian clocks
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A Goodwin/Leloup-Goldbeter delayed-feedback oscillator with entrainment and a jet-lag payoff is real level-3 content that visitors want, though its oscillator lesson overlaps the repressilator half of genetic-circuits.

build 5: A Goodwin loop or the Leloup-Goldbeter model (BioModels, CC0) is a small ODE; entrainment, phase shifts after a jet-lag jump and the loss of rhythm when the delay is short all come out of integrating it.

runnersUp.title: Counting & probability trees
judgeNotes: build 5: Multiplying along branches, a seeded Monte Carlo tally, path counting for Pascal's triangle and the birthday product are exact and trivial to compute; the model is real and needs no data.

fit-level 4: Probability trees and drawing with or without replacement are core school probability that bayes-theorem and central-limit-theorem don't cover. Running the experiment against the tree's prediction makes a proper interactive mechanism.

runnersUp.title: Thermostat
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: On/off control with a hysteresis wobble and the 'turning it up doesn't heat faster' takeaway is a good level-0 precursor to feedback-control without duplicating PID.

build 5: Newton's law of cooling plus a heater with a hysteresis switch is a one-line ODE that shows the wobble band, overshoot and on-time responding to every control; this is the honest model at this level.

runnersUp.title: Why hot things glow
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A real mechanism (the blackbody law turned into a visible colour) built on familiar objects (toaster, bulb, Sun), honest at level 0, and distinct, since stars only uses colour as one detail.

build 5: Planck's law through the CIE CMFs and blackBody routine the site already ships is a small, honest, real-time model, it needs no new data, and an infrared false-colour view can be computed from the same spectrum.

runnersUp.title: The coalescent
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The standard backward-in-time population-genetics model, with a mechanism the stepping graphic shows well (lineages merging, bottleneck collapse), and distinct from forward-time population genetics; it is more abstract for general visitors.

build 5: A backward Wright-Fisher simulation of ten lineages with mutations dropped on the branches is trivial to run in a browser, and the scaling with population size and the effect of a bottleneck are direct output of the model.

runnersUp.title: What an average hides
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The mean as a balance point that an outlier drags while the median stays put is a physical, visible mechanism with everyday value, and no existing page shows it.
build 5: A plank tipping about a fulcrum by net torque of coin stacks finds the mean physically, with the median computed alongside: a small, honest lever model with no data.

runnersUp.title: Mechanical clocks & escapements
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A mechanism the eye can follow, plus real level-3 content (circular error, Airy's condition on impulse timing), distinct from oscillations-resonance's sinusoidal drive.
build 5: A nonlinear pendulum ODE with an impulse applied at a chosen phase directly shows the circular error and Airy's escapement-error result. It needs no data and is small and honest.

runnersUp.title: Stopping a car: twice the speed, four times the skid
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Thinking distance plus braking distance, with doubling the speed quadrupling the braking part, is a concrete and useful mechanism that a level-0 reader can grasp as a comparison; distinct from newtons-laws and from the other car candidates.
build 5: Reaction distance plus v²/(2μg) is the honest model, the doubling and quadrupling are visible on the strip, and the rule 126 figures are Crown copyright published under OGL v3 on GOV.UK.

runnersUp.title: How a simulation works
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Stepping a ball and an orbit, with step-size error and the half-step update fixing the orbit, is the site's own engine made visible and honest at level 1, and neither calculus nor any physics page shows it.

build 5: Explicit Euler versus semi-implicit (symplectic) stepping on a falling ball and a Kepler orbit against the exact solution is the honest, tiny model, and the error and energy drift are visible on the graphic.

runnersUp.title: Locks, races & deadlock
judgeNotes: build 5: Interleavings of two threads and dining philosophers with a resource-allocation graph and cycle detection make a small, deterministic simulation that is clearly visible.
fit-level 4: Races, locks and a resource-graph cycle in dining philosophers form a clear, simulable mechanism that is core to university concurrency courses, and no existing page covers it.

runnersUp.title: Statistics: averages, spread & correlation
judgeNotes: build 5: Live mean, median, r and least squares on draggable points cost nothing to compute; Anscombe's 44 numbers are published facts, and Palmer penguins is confirmed CC0 and gives a real hidden-variable scatter.

fit-level 4: Dragging points to move the mean, median and r, plus Anscombe's quartet and a confounder, are much-wanted ideas at an honest level 1. It only touches learning-from-data at the fitted line, and its takeaway is about what r means, which is distinct.

runnersUp.title: Quorum sensing
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Diffusion plus LuxI/LuxR positive feedback giving a collective threshold switch is a showable mechanism distinct from crispr and lac-operon, and appealing as glowing bacteria.
build 5: Cells on a grid secreting a diffusing, decaying signal with a Hill-type LuxR switch make a small reaction-diffusion and agent model that shows the collective switch directly.

runnersUp.title: Solitons
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: KdV steepening balanced against dispersion, with the defining collision test, is a clear mechanism distinct from linear waves-interference.

build 5: An event-driven elastic-collision model computes each collision exactly (314 for ratio 10^4 is trivial), and the velocity-space circle view is a direct transform of the same state.

runnersUp.title: Wind-up toys
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Stored turns spent through a gear train is a fine mechanism, but its speed-versus-duration trade echoes the other simple-machine candidates.

build 5: Spring torque falling with the turns left, a gear ratio, leg friction and a fan governor with speed-squared drag make a small ODE that shows the fast-short against slow-long trade and the steadying effect directly.

runnersUp.title: Sizing grid storage
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Its diminishing-returns curve over a year of real data is a genuine level-3 analysis, but it is more of a data study than a mechanism, and it extends power-grid's battery rather than showing something new.

build 5: 8760 hours of public-domain EIA-930 data with a greedy charge/discharge rule is tiny to ship and to run. Sweeping storage size to draw the unmet-demand curve is real computation, not a picture.

runnersUp.title: Continued fractions & rational approximation
judgeNotes: build 5: The expansion is the Euclidean algorithm, and the rectangle cutting, convergents and lattice points are exact constructions; the Metonic example needs only the published lengths of the month and year, which are facts.

fit-level 3: Cutting squares from a rectangle and finding best rational approximations is a nice mechanism and distinct from existing pages. It needs only fractions, so level 2 is more honest than 3, and its demand is narrower than the core topics.

runnersUp.title: Electric vehicle drivetrains
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An honest level-3 vehicle energy balance with a useful takeaway about drag and regenerative braking, but it is more an energy-accounting simulation than one mechanism and spreads across motor, pack and road.

build 5: Road-load equations, a motor torque-speed envelope and an internal-resistance pack integrated over a public-domain EPA drive cycle make a small, real time-stepped model with an observable energy and range result.

runnersUp.title: A solar panel through the day
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The angle of sunlight on a panel is a real, manipulable effect, but it largely reuses sun-earth-moon's cosine idea applied to a panel, so it is a modest addition.

build 5: NOAA's solar-position equations (public domain), the cosine of the angle between the sun and the panel's normal, and a published clear-sky model give an honest, cheap model of output by hour and by year.

runnersUp.title: Electrode kinetics: Nernst to Butler-Volmer
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Butler-Volmer and cyclic voltammetry are genuine level-3 electrochemistry, but specialist and less appealing to visitors, and it partly overlaps the corrosion candidate's mixed-potential material.

build 5: A 1D diffusion grid with a Butler-Volmer boundary is the standard way to simulate cyclic voltammetry, cheap enough to run live, and it reproduces the Nernst ratio, the Tafel slope, the peaks growing with the square root of the sweep rate and the diffusion limit from a few textbook constants.

runnersUp.title: Momentum, impulse & crashes
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Impulse and crumple zones are worth a page, but newtons-laws already collides carts to show momentum conservation, so only the impulse, elasticity and angled-collision steps are new.

build 5: 1D collisions with a coefficient of restitution, a spring-damper contact giving a force-time pulse whose area is conserved, recoil and 2D billiard collisions are small, honest mechanics models with no data needed.

runnersUp.title: How a computer flips a coin
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A deterministic rule on a wheel that repeats is a real mechanism a child can follow, but 'multiply, add, keep the last two digits' borders on arithmetic, and the leadsTo of epidemics is a weak fit (binary or cryptography would fit better).
build 5: A tiny linear congruential generator, with its period and the replay from the same seed, is the exact model, trivially interactive.

runnersUp.title: Linear programming & the simplex method
judgeNotes: build 5: Half-plane intersection, a sliding objective line, simplex pivots on a tiny tableau and a projected 3D polytope are all exact and small; this is the real algorithm.
fit-level 3: Simplex walking polygon corners is a clear, useful level-3 mechanism. It depends on convex-duality and overlaps it on shadow prices, so the two should split that material.

runnersUp.title: Why a spinning top stays up
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Gyroscopic precession can be shown well from the real equations, but why spin turns a tip into a wobble cannot honestly be explained without vectors, so at level 0 it risks being a demonstration rather than an understanding.

build 5: The heavy symmetric top with friction torque is a few ODEs that integrate in real time and genuinely produce precession, nutation and the eventual topple; the model is upper-level, but what the reader sees is level 0.

runnersUp.title: Epigenetic memory
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The real Dodd et al. model at an honest level, but it is niche and its bistable-memory takeaway is largely the same as lac-operon's, cell-cycle-switch's and the toggle switch's in this file.

build 5: The Dodd et al. 2007 stochastic nucleosome model (about 60 sites, recruited conversions, halving at division) is small and runs in real time, and bistability, memory and its loss when cooperativity is weak emerge from the model.

runnersUp.title: The genetic code's error tolerance
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An interesting computational result (the real code against shuffled codes), but it is a scoring analysis more than a mechanism in motion, and its appeal is narrower than the other level-3 candidates.

build 5: Scoring thousands of block-preserving random codes against amino-acid property scales (20 published values each, which are facts) is a fast algorithm, and the histogram with the standard code far in the tail is visible without reading any text.

runnersUp.title: Earth's magnetic field & the geodynamo
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An honest level-3 spherical-harmonic decomposition of IGRF, but it explores data rather than modelling the geodynamo the title promises, and it shares ground with the compass candidate.

build 5: Summing a spherical harmonic series from IGRF-14 coefficients (freely distributed by NCEI and IAGA; the numbers are facts) for each epoch from 1900 to 2025, with degree truncation, is cheap in the browser, and the polarity time scale is a small table of published chron boundaries.

runnersUp.title: Winding numbers & the fundamental theorem of algebra
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An elegant topological proof with a draggable mechanism and an honest level-3 pitch, but its audience is narrower than the other math candidates.

build 5: Accumulating the argument along a dragged loop and mapping circles through a polynomial are exact, cheap geometry, and the integer jump at the crossing and the image passing through the origin are directly visible.

runnersUp.title: Pseudo-random numbers
judgeNotes: build 5: LCG, RANDU, xorshift and live chi-square and serial tests are a few lines of code each; the RANDU planes in a rotatable 3D cloud are an honest, striking result.
fit-level 3: The RANDU planes and live statistical tests make a good visual reveal and the subject is distinct from chaos-fractals, but it is less in demand, and the core idea could sit at level 2.

runnersUp.title: How dunes march
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A real grain-saltation-and-avalanche model whose emergent dunes are lovely, though it has a lower curriculum demand and is a cousin of the river and sand candidates.
build 5: Werner's 1995 slab model (saltation hops, shadow zones, avalanching at the angle of repose) is a tiny cellular model that grows real dune shapes in seconds in the browser.

runnersUp.title: Repeat: loops
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A genuine, Logo-style mechanism that is honest at level 0, but it reuses robot-instructions' cards and robot, so it reads more like that page's second half than a separate topic; keep it only if both survive as a pair.
build 5: A turtle-graphics interpreter with nested repeat cards is a genuine, tiny program runner whose drawn path is a pure function of step count; no data.

runnersUp.title: Inside a lithium-ion cell under load
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The single-particle model with diffusion-limited surface concentration and lithium plating is the real level-3 electrochemistry and distinct from redox-batteries' cartoon, but it overlaps battery-degradation and should merge with it or take precedence over it.

build 5: A single-particle model (two spherical diffusion PDEs on a few dozen radial nodes, Butler-Volmer, OCP curves) runs easily in real time. Parameters come from the BSD-licensed PyBaMM Chen2020 set, taken from an open-access paper, and the plating threshold emerges from the anode potential.

runnersUp.title: Numerical methods & stability
judgeNotes: build 5: Four integrators on small ODEs, stability regions drawn as level sets of |R(z)| and an explicit heat solver blowing up past the CFL limit are exactly the honest model, and all are cheap.

fit-level 3: Stability regions and stiff problems are real level-3 numerical analysis with a vivid blow-up demo. It overlaps the Euler step-size material in differential-equations and appeals to a narrower audience.

runnersUp.title: Hartree-Fock: the self-consistent field
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The self-consistent-field loop is real university quantum chemistry and is showable, but it is abstract and niche for this site's visitors, and it depends on the proposed huckel page.

build 5: STO-3G H2 and HeH+ (the Szabo and Ostlund example) need 2x2 matrices and analytic s-Gaussian integrals, so the SCF loop, the bond-length scan and the exact two-determinant comparison all run instantly; the dozen basis numbers are published facts, whatever the Basis Set Exchange data licence.

runnersUp.title: Lambda calculus & types
judgeNotes: build 5: A beta-reducer with normal-order stepping, Church encodings and a simple type checker is a small honest algorithm that runs instantly in the browser; omega needs a step cap.

fit-level 3: A real mechanism (beta reduction, Church numerals, Y combinator, typing) that shows well step by step and is distinct from turing-machines, but it is the narrowest audience in the batch and its payoff is abstract.

runnersUp.title: The microbiome as an ecosystem
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Generalised Lotka-Volterra with inferred interactions and alternative stable states is a real level-3 mechanism distinct from the ecosystems page, though a ten-group matrix is hard to make legible.
build 5: A ten-species generalized Lotka-Volterra ODE with an antibiotic term is tiny, and Stein et al. 2013 publish the fitted matrix in PLOS Computational Biology under CC BY.

runnersUp.title: Noise in gene expression
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A real Gillespie model with the elegant two-reporter scatter, but it is specialised and partly repeated by the stochastic-solver step of genetic-circuits.

build 5: A Gillespie simulation of the telegraph model for a thousand cells is cheap, especially if precomputed per parameter change, and the bursts, the widening histogram and the two-reporter split into intrinsic and extrinsic noise are real model output.

runnersUp.title: Dialysis: a kidney from a membrane
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Countercurrent mass transfer and the urea sawtooth are a real mechanism, but the page leans on kidney-nephron and repeats its countercurrent idea, so it is better as a closing section of that page than as a page of its own.
build 5: Countercurrent versus cocurrent mass transfer has closed-form solutions, and single-pool urea kinetics is a one-line ODE; typical KoA and flow values are textbook numbers.

runnersUp.title: Cosmic rays & air showers
judgeNotes: build 4: The Heitler-Matthews branching cascade is a small, exact toy model that shows N_max proportional to E and the elongation rate; Auger open data are released on Zenodo under CC BY-SA 4.0, so the data are openly licensed (the entry's 'not confirmed' can be updated).

runnersUp.title: From base model to assistant
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: It shows concretely, with chat templates, answer-only loss and side-by-side distributions, how a base model becomes an assistant, which is a key gap in the LLM story; showing behaviour needs two small open models in the browser.

build 3: SmolLM2-135M base and Instruct are Apache-2.0 with official ONNX/Transformers.js builds, but running two in the page is a multi-hundred-MB download, so precomputed next-token distributions are the practical form. The 'step through the template' part risks becoming a browse-a-diagram.

runnersUp.title: Where a language model keeps its facts
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Causal tracing is a real intervention with a clear heatmap and asks a different question from the logit lens (what causes recall, not what is readable). It is more specialised, but valuable for a detailed LLM series.

build 3: Causal tracing can be precomputed for GPT-2 small, but the page becomes exploring a fixed heatmap rather than driving a live model. GPT-2 small recalls facts weakly (the original work used GPT-2 XL), so the effect must be checked on the chosen prompts before committing.

runnersUp.title: How a phone knows your finger
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Matching ridge endings and forks against an 'enough' line is a clean level-0 mechanism on a familiar object, and nothing existing shows a biometric match; it is the stronger of the two biometric candidates.

build 3: Minutiae alignment and counting is a real, small algorithm. Synthesising ridges SFinGe-style (orientation field plus Gabor filtering) and thinning them is substantial work, best precomputed. It is correct that no real fingerprint database is openly licensed.

runnersUp.title: Training reasoning with checkable rewards
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: It applies policy-gradient RL with group-relative advantages to a language model and shows pass@1 rising against pass@k, which is distinct from the grid-world RL page and central to modern reasoning models, though live GRPO in the browser is ambitious.

build 3: GRPO on a tiny model needs a group of sampled attempts plus a policy-gradient step per puzzle, so only a very short run is interactive and the rest must be precomputed checkpoints. The pass@1-rises-while-pass@64-stays effect has to be reproduced on the project's own tiny model first, and it may not show at this scale.

runnersUp.title: Growing patterns & doubling
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Adding the same against doubling, side by side, is a strong level-0 toy that fills the gap left by the reserved exponentials topic; epidemics shows doubling only inside a disease model.

build 3: Linear versus doubling sequences with tiles, a chart and a folding counter are trivially computable and honest, but the model is very thin and the 'chart leaves the screen' needs a deliberate scale design.

runnersUp.title: Where the energy in a circuit really flows
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A well-known counter-intuitive result with a clear field mechanism, distinct from electric-circuits; its time-domain part overlaps maxwell-equations, so the two need a clean split.

build 3: Possible but approximate: in-plane E from a Laplace solve with Biot-Savart B normal to the plane gives an in-plane Poynting field, but a 2D Laplace solve treats the wires as sheets, and the light-second time-domain run needs a scaled-down FDTD whose transient size depends on geometry, so it must avoid overclaiming.

runnersUp.title: The water cycle

build 3: A Markov-chain particle model between stores is buildable, but with a few hundred dots the true USGS shares (about 0.001 percent in the air) put no dots in the air or rivers, so the visible clouds and rivers contradict the counter unless the page uses a log scale or labels the over-represented stores.

runnersUp.title: The CMB power spectrum

runnersUp.title: Bread and yeast

build 3: Yeast agents that consume sugar at a cardinal-temperature rate and produce gas filling bubbles are buildable. Dough expansion from gas volume is reasonable, but the baking stage (oven spring, crumb setting) would be scripted, and the fermentation study is not named.

runnersUp.title: Why a cut apple goes brown
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A familiar object with one-control experiments (acid, air, cold, heat) showing an enzyme at work is a good level-0 toy, though its 'heat destroys the enzyme' beat overlaps jelly-and-pineapple.

build 3: An oxygen-diffusion grid with an enzyme rate that depends on pH and temperature is an honest small reaction-diffusion model. However, the PPO constants are only gestured at ('polyphenol-oxidase references'), and with one control per region the result is close to a set of rate multipliers, so a concrete source for the rate-versus-pH/T curve should be named.

runnersUp.title: Zoom by tens
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Powers of ten as clicks of a dial with true-scale fit counts is a strong level-0 explorer, distinct from deep-time's timeline and from the-cell's zoom through one cell.

build 3: A log-scale true-size renderer over a cited sizes table is buildable and the NASA NSSDC fact sheet is public domain, but the 'model' is mostly a lookup and the page risks becoming a browse-a-shelf unless the fit counting and click counts stay central.

runnersUp.title: How a seed wakes up
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A classic primary-school experiment with a surprising, showable takeaway (sprouts in the dark, mass falls before leaves open); clearly the stage before photosynthesis, so it doesn't overlap that page.

build 3: Hydrothermal time sets when the seed germinates and a reserve-versus-photosynthesis mass balance gives the dip-then-rise curve, both real and small; but the root and shoot turning and the pale growth in the dark are drawn rather than modelled (the entry itself says the model has no light term), so part of the page is a scripted picture.

runnersUp.title: Auroras: the Sun's wind on Earth's magnet
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Charged specks sliding along field lines into polar rings works without formulas and has one control and a well-known sky phenomenon; leadsTo should point to something nearer than atoms-periodic-table (for example sun-earth-moon), since electromagnetism is level 2.

build 3: Integrating particles in a dipole compressed by solar-wind pressure does not produce the auroral oval (that needs tail and reconnection physics), so the stated model risks being a staged picture that teaches direct-entry; an honest L0 version would drive the oval from an empirical model (e.g. Feldstein/OVATION, public domain) with the guiding-centre spiral as an illustration.

runnersUp.title: Soap: surfactants & micelles
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Self-assembly with a CMC kink and packing-driven sphere-to-bilayer shapes is real colloid science behind an everyday object (soap), distinct from the-cell's static membrane.

build 3: A 2D lattice Monte Carlo of amphiphiles (Larson-type) can show interface adsorption and a CMC kink at interactive rates. However, the shift from spheres to bilayers with head/tail size and oil solubilisation are hard to obtain reliably in 2D, so the scope should be narrowed to the CMC and the interface.

runnersUp.title: Tidal locking & orbital resonance
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The secular tidal evolution into tidal locking and the Laplace resonance is a real long-timescale mechanism that sun-earth-moon's present-day tides do not show.

build 3: The secular tidal equations for spin and orbit are easy, but capturing the 2:1 chain and the Laplace resonance needs an orbit-resolving N-body run with a parametrised migration force and compressed timescales, which is buildable but harder to keep honest.

runnersUp.title: Water drops & surface tension
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Beading, the coin bulge, the floating paperclip and soap are classic, hands-on surface-tension mechanics absent from states-of-matter; it is distinct from the sponge candidate if that one sticks to adhesion and capillarity.

build 3: A 2D molecular box with a free surface and a tunable wall attraction honestly shows beading and wetting, but the coin bulge, floating paperclip, pond skater and pepper are macroscopic effects that the particle box cannot reach at its scale, so those scenes need a separate Young-Laplace model or should be cut.

runnersUp.title: Zipper
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Interlocking teeth and the slider's wedge are a visual, little-known mechanism a child handles daily; there is nothing like it on the site.

build 3: The Y-channel engaging the teeth is a buildable geometric construction, but the pull test is thin: the load share is simple division and the open-stretch case has no real model, so the page leans toward an animation of a mechanism.

runnersUp.title: How plants drink
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Transpiration pull from the dyed-celery experiment, with weather as the control, is a genuine mechanism for beginners that photosynthesis does not show.

build 3: Flow set by evaporative demand (light, wind, humidity, stomatal opening), with the dye front advected at that rate, is honest but simple, essentially a demand formula plus advection. The leaf-pore zoom and the tree-scale bucket count are illustrations rather than model output.

runnersUp.title: TLS: how a connection becomes private
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A real protocol mechanism (key share, certificate chain, forward secrecy) with a strong MITM toggle, honestly level 3 and distinct from cryptography's separate primitives, though its prerequisite elliptic-curve-cryptography is only a pool candidate.

runnersUp.title: Galois theory: why the quintic has no formula
judgeNotes: build 3: Tracking the roots numerically while the coefficients move and recording the permutation is buildable and honest, but Arnold's nested-commutator argument for degree 5 needs carefully precomputed loops, and the commutator depth is an argument the page shows rather than a model it computes, so this is a hard page to make legible.

fit-level 4: Arnold's topological proof, with roots permuting as coefficients loop, is a rare case where a deep theorem gets a genuine animated mechanism. It is a distinctive level-3 draw, though hard to build well.

runnersUp.title: How a web page is drawn
judgeNotes: build 3: Buildable only with a deliberately tiny HTML subset parser, selector matcher and block/inline layout engine; the scope is large and risks a stepped diagram, so it must restrict itself to a stated subset of CSS.
fit-level 4: Parsing, style matching, layout and paint form a real pipeline that a level-1 reader can follow on editable HTML, and the page picks up where the internet page stops.

runnersUp.title: Heat transfer: conduction, convection & radiation
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A much-wanted, honest level-1 mechanism page (heat through a wall, convection cells, radiation) that no existing page shows, since entropy only equalises particle temperatures; trim it to the wall and keep the pan and radiator as short steps so it stays one graphic.

build 3: The conduction core is an honest, small 1D/2D heat equation on a grid through a wall with a tabulated k (facts, no licence issue). The pan-convection, radiator and thermal-camera add-ons are not modelled, though: honest convection needs a fluid solver, and the others are pictures. Narrow it to the wall/insulation model with a U-value meter.

runnersUp.title: How a broken bone mends
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A clear staged mechanism (haematoma, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling) with one honest control (cast vs movement) that a 10-year-old who has seen a cast will follow; distinct from bridges-structures and from the level-3 bone-remodelling candidate.

build 3: A grid where callus ossifies where strain is low and is resorbed where unloaded is a real (if crude) mechanobiology rule and runs easily, but the hematoma-callus-remodel stages risk being a scripted timeline rather than an outcome of the rule; the build must make the non-union and thin-bone results emerge from the grid.

runnersUp.title: Mantle convection
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A Rayleigh-number convection box with a stagnant lid and Nusselt scaling is the real model behind plate-tectonics and is clearly university geophysics.

build 3: Isoviscous infinite-Prandtl convection (a streamfunction biharmonic solved by FFT or multigrid on about 128x64) is interactive, but the stagnant-lid and plate-like regimes need viscosity contrasts of 10^4 or more and fine grids at high Rayleigh number, so the solve is stiff and slow; limit the contrast range and precompute the Nusselt-Rayleigh plot, or the lid-foundering part will not run live.

runnersUp.title: Tap to pay
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A battery-less card powered by the reader's pulsing magnetism is an everyday mystery with a clear mechanism of power against distance, kept simpler than and distinct from electromagnetism.

build 3: Coupling between coaxial loops against distance with a wake-up threshold is honest but thin: mostly one meter against distance. 'Stack two cards and the reader cannot tell them apart' is wrong, because ISO 14443 anticollision tells cards apart and payment terminals detect the clash and refuse; it also cites a metal-detector page that is not in this batch.

runnersUp.title: What a fire needs
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Fuel-heat-air with one control removed at a time is a standard primary-school topic with a clear mechanism, distinct from the level-2 reaction-rates page; absorb the jar-weight idea from candle-under-a-jar.
build 3: The oxygen-depletion part is a real small model, but the water, wet-cloth and wick-cutting controls are rule toggles. It is nearly the same page as candle-under-a-jar, so merge them.

runnersUp.title: Cooking an egg
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Proteins unfolding and tangling irreversibly with heat is a clear mechanism from a universal experience, distinct from level-2 protein-folding, with a single thermometer control.

build 3: Threshold denaturation temperatures are published facts, so it is buildable. But the honest model needs heat conduction into the egg over time (time-at-temperature, first-order kinetics), not a dragged thermometer. The grey ring (iron sulfide) is not modelled.

runnersUp.title: Electrolysis
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Electrolysis is core secondary-school chemistry with a clear particle mechanism; it is the reverse of redox-batteries and adds the discharge rules and the charge-to-mass relation.

build 3: Ion drift and charge counting (Faraday) are a real, small particle model, but which ion is discharged in solution comes from a lookup rule in the reactivity series rather than from the model, and the aluminium-cell coda is a picture; data are only reference constants.

runnersUp.title: Superconductivity

build 3: The London-equation grid, the numerical BCS gap equation and an RCSJ junction ODE are each buildable, but zero resistance would just be set rather than modelled, and four loosely joined models risk becoming a slideshow; it needs narrowing to one or two mechanisms.

runnersUp.title: Why some volcanoes explode and others ooze
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Viscosity trapping gas, shown as fizz versus burst, is the mechanism plate-tectonics never shows and works with one control for a 10-year-old.

build 3: Decompression bubble growth, Stokes rise of bubbles through a magma of chosen viscosity, and fragmentation above about 75 percent gas fraction can be computed in a 1D conduit, but the model is coarse and risks becoming a two-ending story unless the eruption style follows from the computed gas fraction.

runnersUp.title: Why onions make you cry
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A familiar experience explained by one clear mechanism (cutting a cell mixes two separated ingredients), with honest single-variable remedies, at level 0, and distinct from the-cell.

runnersUp.title: Why leaves change colour

build 3: Three pigment pools driven by day length, temperature and light, with leaf colour mixed from the pigment fractions, can be built and gives an honest qualitative model for level 0, but the rate constants have no source and the result is close to a scripted colour ramp; mixing from measured absorption spectra (licence to check) would make it more than a picture.

runnersUp.title: The nitrogen cycle

build 3: The bacterial agent model is buildable but its rates are invented, which makes it a dressed-up diagram, and adding eutrophication puts a second model on the page; the Fowler et al. 2013 licence is unconfirmed, so build a stoichiometric box model with literature rates and a qualitative diagram, or scale it down.

runnersUp.title: Mass, binding energy & the valley of stability

build 3: The AME2020/NUBASE2020 values are freely downloadable facts and the papers are CC BY 3.0, but the files carry no licence and only ask for citation, which leaves the data partly unconfirmed. As described, the page is mostly a chart to browse; adding a semi-empirical mass formula the reader can fit against the data would make it a real model.

runnersUp.title: Electricity at home

But the earth-fault and breaker scenes are rule-driven animations rather than a model, so the page risks being a picture to tap unless the fault path is computed as a real circuit.

runnersUp.title: Where your food goes
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A core primary curriculum topic with a staged mechanism (where each juice acts, absorption in the small intestine), distinct from homeostasis's blood-glucose view.

build 3: A compartment model with first-order breakdown and absorption is buildable, but the rates are rough textbook figures and the page leans toward a scripted scrub-through of a diagram; it needs the food-dependent emptying and breakdown to come from the model.

runnersUp.title: Taking a mixture apart
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A curriculum staple turned into a genuine build puzzle where each tool exploits one difference between particles, distinct from every existing page.

build 3: A rule-based particle sort through a chain of tools is honest at level 0 but closer to a puzzle state machine than a physical model. The chromatography strip could use real retention factors to give it substance.

runnersUp.title: Bubbles and foam
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A real mechanism (surface tension pulling a film to least area) no existing page shows, with a pokeable film that is a great level-0 toy; arguably physics rather than chemistry.

build 3: A 2D closed film under tension and inside pressure relaxes to a circle, and two bubbles form a flat wall (Plateau), so those parts are buildable. Why plain water fails and soap holds (Marangoni stabilisation) and foam drainage are not captured honestly by a spring mesh, so narrow the page to the least-surface shape.

runnersUp.title: Autoencoders & variational autoencoders
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A navigable latent plane and the KL trade-off are a real mechanism distinct from diffusion's denoising, though it is a second generative-model page alongside diffusion-models.

build 4: Shipping a 2-D-latent AE and VAE trained offline on Fashion-MNIST (MIT) and running the decoders live is honest and small; the KL-weight slider needs a precomputed family of models (or a set of retrained checkpoints) since retraining on images live is too slow, which the entry should state.

runnersUp.title: How a phone counts your steps
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A threshold on a real accelerometer trace is an honest level-0 mechanism with a nice false-positive and false-negative trade-off, but it is thin and is signal processing more than AI.

build 4: Threshold and peak detection on real labelled HAPT accelerometer traces from UCI (CC BY 4.0, UCI's standard licence) is an honest, small model, and the entry is candid that there is no step ground truth and that the car trace is synthetic.

runnersUp.title: Normalizing flows
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Honest level 3 with a vivid change-of-variables graphic, but a niche generative family that fewer visitors will look for than VAEs or diffusion.

build 4: Affine coupling layers in 2-D have exact Jacobians and train on two-moons in seconds with hand-written gradients or a tiny autodiff; the density recoloring is an honest change-of-variables evaluation on a grid.

runnersUp.title: Why the app says 'you might also like'
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Co-visitation counts with a popularity pull and a cold-start problem form a real but thin mechanism, it sits close to pagerank's link-graph picture, and it repeats the batch's 'it's just counting' theme.

build 4: Item-to-item counts from a small CC0 Wikimedia Clickstream subset (licence confirmed) is an honest recommender, and following arrows is a real random walk that drifts toward hubs. It must keep the computation (drift, cold start) visible so it doesn't become a graph to browse.

runnersUp.title: How a speaker hears its name
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Building the spectrogram is a good visual, but the deciding step is a black-box network with confidence bars, so the page shows less mechanism than its level-0 siblings; it is still distinct from convolution-vision.

build 4: The TF.js speech-commands model (Apache 2.0, 18-word vocabulary) and Speech Commands clips (CC BY 4.0) run in the browser. The network itself is a black box, the shipped clips have to be pushed through the same WebAudio spectrogram pipeline the model expects, and the page adds a TF.js dependency.

runnersUp.title: Federated learning & differential privacy
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Federated averaging with client drift and a privacy-noise trade-off is a valid level-3 mechanism, but it is niche and bundles two topics (federation and differential privacy).

build 4: FedAvg over a few simulated clients with small 2-D models, plus clipping and Gaussian noise, is cheap and honest. The privacy budget slider must compute a real epsilon (for example from a moments accountant or a simple Gaussian-mechanism bound) rather than a label.

runnersUp.title: Distillation: a small model learning from a large one
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A real mechanism (soft targets at a temperature) with a clean comparison of loss curves, but it is less central to understanding LLMs than its siblings and partly repeats the training page's loss-curve race.

build 4: A shipped teacher (own weights) plus two small students training live on Tiny Shakespeare is feasible, and the soft-target bars are exact. The gap between the two loss curves must be measured on the real tiny models, since at this scale it may be small.

runnersUp.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: In high demand and its ranking is live, but the generation half is precomputed and the page is more a pipeline than one mechanism, which leans toward the embeddings and language-models pages.

build 4: BM25 and MiniLM embedding search over a few thousand CC BY-SA paragraphs run in the browser (Apache-2.0 model via transformers.js or precomputed vectors), and the answers with and without retrieval are honestly precomputed from an open small model for a fixed question set; the free-question path shows only retrieval, which should be stated.

runnersUp.title: World models & model-based RL
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The compounding error of imagined rollouts is a clear level-3 mechanism beyond grid-world RL, but it needs a live dynamics model plus a planner, which is heavy for its audience.

build 4: Cart-pole dynamics, a small MLP learning the next state online and Dyna- or MPC-style planning in imagination all run at interactive rates, and compounding model error is a real outcome of the learned model.

runnersUp.title: Dropout, weight decay & batch normalization
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Each technique is real, but bundling dropout, weight decay and batch norm reads as a survey of training tricks rather than one mechanism with one takeaway; it would be stronger narrowed to a single technique.

build 4: A small MLP on 2-D data trained live, TensorFlow-Playground style, with dropout, weight decay and batch norm is fully buildable. The many synchronised panels (boundary, histograms, per-layer activations) are a scope risk, not a buildability one.

runnersUp.title: Induction heads & in-context learning
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A real, testable circuit (shown by ablation) that is distinct from transformers, but it is research-frontier interpretability rather than what a typical university student learns, and it depends on precomputed training checkpoints.

build 4: A two-layer attention-only transformer with a tiny vocabulary is cheap to run forward and to ablate in the browser. The phase-change checkpoints must be trained offline (feasible on a laptop), with own weights and no external data.

runnersUp.title: Telescopes
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A good mechanism page (aperture and the diffraction limit) that is distinct from light-optics, but it is honestly level 2, the level the plan wants least, and it borders aperture-synthesis.

build 4: Ray tracing plus a computed Airy pattern on a synthetic star field, with seeing as a blur kernel, is all client-side and needs no data; it is broad (five sub-scenes) and should be scoped tightly.

runnersUp.title: Where your calories go
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The resting-versus-exercise energy budget is a useful counterintuitive takeaway and honest at level 0, but it is closer to an accounting display than a mechanism the graphic can show, and must avoid diet-advice framing.

build 4: Mifflin-St Jeor, Compendium MET values (numbers, free online) and USDA FoodData Central (public domain) give a real, openly sourced energy budget; buildable as an hourly stacked-block model, though it is closer to an explorable calculator than a simulation.

runnersUp.title: What an asteroid does when it hits
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The atmospheric-entry integration with fragmentation is a real model, but much of the page is published effect scalings drawn as rings, which leans toward a calculator; it is distinct from deep-time.

build 4: Integrating entry with drag, ablation and pancake breakup, then applying the published Collins-Melosh-Marcus scaling laws, is a small honest model; the equations come from a published paper, so no dataset licence is involved.

runnersUp.title: The Dirac equation
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: It is real and distinct, but a 1D Dirac spinor with Zitterbewegung and the Klein paradox is at the edge of graduate material, hard to make legible as a graphic, and appeals to fewer visitors than the core level-3 pages.

build 4: A 1D two-component Dirac packet solved by split-operator FFT is small and fast, and it shows Zitterbewegung and the Klein step honestly; it has to be done in momentum space to avoid fermion doubling on a naive grid.

runnersUp.title: Neutron stars & pulsars
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: The P-Pdot diagram from ATNF data with dipole braking is real and distinct from stars, but it is mostly an explore of a catalogue, with a thinner mechanism than the other space candidates.

build 4: The P-Pdot diagram with dipole formulas and braking tracks is simple and honest; CSIRO's PSRCAT v2 record lists BSD 3-Clause with citation, so the data look reusable, though the catalogue's own site should confirm it.

runnersUp.title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence & photochemistry
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Competing decay routes on a Jablonski diagram are a valid kinetic model, but the graphic is mostly rate-constant bookkeeping with little to see, so its appeal is moderate.

build 4: First-order rate equations, or a stochastic population, for the competing decay routes give the lifetime, quantum yield, phosphorescent tail and Stern-Volmer line exactly; the model is small and honest, if close to a kinetics diagram, and the fluorophore lifetimes and yields are published facts.

runnersUp.title: Origin of life & the error threshold
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Eigen's error threshold is a real mechanism with a clear takeaway, but it is niche, overlaps population-genetics in machinery, and lists a level-3 candidate as a prerequisite.

build 4: A population of bit strings copied with errors on a single-peak landscape runs fast and shows the error threshold honestly; the replicase-evolution, parasite and compartment chapters add scope and should be kept lean.

runnersUp.title: Emoji and text as numbers
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An honest everyday entry point, but its core idea (a character is a number read by convention) is binary's takeaway at a simpler layer, so it is only partly distinct; the empty-box and SMS-counter details keep it worthwhile.

build 4: Encoding text to code points and to the GSM 7-bit or UCS-2 segment rules is real and small, and Unicode data is permissively licensed; the page must count an emoji as a surrogate pair (two UCS-2 units) so the counter is right.

runnersUp.title: Databases & queries
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Tables, keys, joins and indexes fill a real gap and the index row-count is a visible mechanism, but the page tries to cover normalisation, queries, indexes and transactions at once, and transactions overlap b-trees-transactions, so it should be trimmed to keys, joins and the index.

build 4: A tiny in-browser relational engine (filter, sort, hash/nested-loop join, index vs full scan with row counts) over Palmer penguins (CC0) or a GeoNames extract (CC BY 4.0) is real and fast; the concurrent-transaction scene needs to be a real interleaving, not a canned animation.

runnersUp.title: Maglev trains
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Eddy-current lift and drag against speed, and the unstable attractive design held by feedback, are real mechanisms, but they are two half-topics, and the second leans on feedback-control.

build 4: The analytic thin-sheet electrodynamic lift and drag formulas against speed, plus an unstable EMS ODE with a tunable controller, are small and honest. The drawn eddy-current pattern should come from the analytic solution, not be decoration.

runnersUp.title: Renormalization: the same picture at every scale
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Block-spin coarse-graining is a real and visual idea, but it is applied to the same Ising snapshots and could be a final step of ising-model rather than its own page.

build 4: Majority-rule 3x3 blocking of Ising snapshots is trivial, but critical snapshots on a 243- or 729-wide lattice need a Wolff cluster sampler or precomputed configurations, and the 'flow' plot is a correlation proxy, not a true coupling flow.

runnersUp.title: Satellites: the ones that race and the one that stays
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Ground tracks, the geostationary height and dusk visibility are appealing and distinct from orbits-kepler, but there are too many ideas and views for a one-control level-0 page; it should be trimmed to one takeaway.

build 4: Circular orbits over a rotating Earth give ground tracks, and a shadow-cylinder test gives visibility at dusk; this is honest geometry, ISS elements from NASA are public domain, and generic altitudes suffice for the other satellites.

runnersUp.title: The mole & reacting masses
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An honest, much-needed level-1 topic with a showable limiting-reagent mechanism, but it is closer to a calculation procedure than a 'how it works' phenomenon.

build 4: Balancing by atom counts, converting grams to moles with IUPAC atomic weights (openly available), and finding the limiting reagent are real algorithms, and the leftover reactant shows on screen; the risk is a worksheet rather than a scene, so the counts must be drawn as molecules.

runnersUp.title: Random walks & Brownian motion
judgeNotes: build 4: Thousands of walkers, root-mean-square growth, a histogram compared with the heat kernel and a self-similar path are easy; the return experiment can only show the fraction returned by time T, which saturates near 0.34 in 3D and creeps toward 1 slowly in 2D, so the page must not claim to show that every walker returns.

fit-level 3: The √t spreading and Pólya's recurrence across dimensions make a good level-3 page. It overlaps central-limit-theorem's Galton board and heat-and-wave-equations' diffusion, so it should lean on the recurrence and scale-invariance material.

runnersUp.title: Fixed points, Newton's method & its fractal
judgeNotes: build 4: Cobwebs and Newton tangents are trivial; the Newton basin image needs per-pixel iteration rendered to a raster image inside the SVG, which is affordable and has precedent in chaos-fractals' Mandelbrot zoom.

fit-level 3: Cobwebs, the role of the slope in convergence, and Newton basins make a sound mechanism at level 3. They sit close to chaos-fractals (cobwebbed logistic map, complex-plane fractal zoom) and partly to numerical-stability.

runnersUp.title: Fireworks: a bag of sparks thrown in every direction
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An appealing hook with a real mechanism (equal-speed stars form a sphere that falls together), but much of it is a sequence of stages and a colour table rather than one strong toy.

build 4: Ballistic shell plus hundreds of star particles with drag is a cheap, honest particle simulation. The metal-to-colour table is factual and easy to cite from an open reference, and NIST ASD is free US-government data with citation, though its licence page was not confirmed.

runnersUp.title: Pain & the gate in the spinal cord
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: A small wired circuit that shows gating and sensitization is a real mechanism, but gate-control theory is a simplified, partly dated model and the page overlaps placebo-expectation's descending modulation.

build 4: A handful of integrate-and-fire neurons with wind-up via facilitation is a small, honest circuit simulation. Gate control is a simplified and partly contested theory, so the page must present it as a model circuit, not established anatomy.

runnersUp.title: Tor & onion routing
judgeNotes: build 4: Layered encryption as a stepped wrap and unwrap is near-diagrammatic, but the Monte Carlo of compromised circuits against the observer's fraction, plus timing correlation, gives it a real model.
fit-level 3: Layered encryption and the odds that an observer controls both ends make a clear, distinct mechanism, but the model is simple enough for a level-2 reader rather than university level.

runnersUp.title: Speed: how far each second
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: Reading speed as the steepness of a distance-time line is honest at level 0 and is not the forces of newtons-laws, but it is a graph-reading lesson more than a mechanism and arguably belongs in physics.
build 4: Constant-speed runners with pauses plotted as distance against ticks is a trivial, honest kinematic model that animates as a pure function of time.

runnersUp.title: Markov chains
