gapEntries.title: Superposition: more features than neurons
gapEntries.interaction: Train a tiny network in the browser to squeeze five input features through two hidden neurons and rebuild them, and see each feature's direction drawn as an arrow in the 2D hidden space. Slide how rarely each feature is active: with dense features the network keeps two of them at right angles and drops the rest; sparser, it packs four as two pairs of opposite arrows; sparser still, the arrows spread into a pentagon that stores all five, at the cost of some interference. Change the importance of each feature and watch which ones lose their arrows.
gapEntries.takeaway: When features are rarely active at the same time, a network stores more of them than it has dimensions by sharing directions among them and accepting some interference, and the arrangement jumps between distinct shapes (two at right angles, opposite pairs, a pentagon) as sparsity grows.
gapEntries.needs: None: the toy model (ReLU output, tied weights, importance-weighted loss) trains in the browser in seconds, as in Elhage et al. 2022, 'Toy Models of Superposition' (Transformer Circuits).
gapEntries.pitfall: The page must not claim that each neuron in a real LLM stands for one concept, nor that this toy proves exactly how large models store facts; superposition is why single neurons are often hard to interpret.
gapEntries.why: 3Blue1Brown's 'How might LLMs store facts' (Deep Learning chapter 7) ends on the superposition hypothesis: https://3blue1brown.substack.com/p/how-might-llms-store-facts-chapter
gapEntries.overlapWith: embeddings: that page shows the directions of pretrained word vectors; this one trains a network live to show how and when it packs more features than dimensions into one space.
gapEntries.needsSource: none (trained in the browser on synthetic data)
gapEntries.verifyNote: The model is the right one: Elhage et al.'s 5-to-2 ReLU toy trains in seconds in the browser. Not a duplicate, and the level and prerequisites are honest. But the takeaway misstates the geometry. In the five-feature pentagon the arrows sit 72 degrees apart, not 'nearly opposite'; opposite (antipodal) pairs belong to an intermediate stage. As sparsity rises, the toy goes from two features at right angles, to two antipodal pairs (four features), to a pentagon of five. The change therefore comes in distinct jumps, not as one switch from 'drop the extras' to 'pack them all in'. The interaction also skips that middle stage.
judgeNotes: build 5: The Elhage et al. 5-to-2 ReLU tied-weight toy model trains in seconds in plain JS, and the antipodal-pair and pentagon geometries are reproducible results that show directly as arrows.
fit-level 4: The toy model of superposition trains live in the browser and shows geometric phase changes, a key interpretability idea that embeddings does not cover, and it is honest at level 3.

gapEntries.title: Drug receptors: dose-response, agonists & antagonists
gapEntries.interaction: Add a drug to a dish of cells and watch it bind receptors by mass action while a log dose-response curve builds point by point; set the drug's affinity and efficacy separately and see potency move the curve sideways while efficacy sets its height. Add a competitive antagonist and the curve slides right in parallel by the Schild ratio, add a non-competitive one and the maximum drops; remove most receptors and a full agonist still gives a full response until its spare receptors run out, while a partial agonist starts blocking the full one.
gapEntries.takeaway: How strongly a drug binds and how strongly it activates are separate properties: a competitive blocker slides the dose-response curve sideways, while a non-competitive one lowers its ceiling once the tissue's spare receptors are used up.
gapEntries.needs: Optional: affinities of a few real agonists and antagonists (e.g. at the beta-adrenergic or mu-opioid receptor) from the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology (database under the Open Database License, ODbL; text content CC BY-SA 4.0). The model itself (operational model, Gaddum-Schild) needs no data.
gapEntries.pitfall: Potency is not efficacy: a more potent drug is not a stronger one, and a maximal response does not mean every receptor is occupied, since many tissues have spare receptors.
gapEntries.why: MIT OCW HST.151 Principles of Pharmacology, lecture 1 'Drug-Receptor Interactions' (mass action, full and partial agonists, reversible and irreversible antagonists): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-151-principles-of-pharmacology-spring-2005/pages/lecture-notes/
gapEntries.overlapWith: pharmacokinetics-dosing (proposed) follows how the body moves a drug's concentration over time; this page is pharmacodynamics, what that concentration does at the receptor, with agonism, antagonism and spare receptors.
gapEntries.needsSource: none required; optional IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology data, ODbL (database) / CC BY-SA 4.0 (text)
gapEntries.verifyNote: The model (mass action, the operational model, Gaddum-Schild) is sound and distinct from pharmacokinetics-dosing, but three things need small changes. (1) The takeaway says a non-competitive blocker lowers the ceiling, which contradicts the page's own spare-receptor feature. With a receptor reserve, an irreversible or non-competitive antagonist first shifts the curve right and lowers the maximum only once the reserve is used up (Furchgott analysis). (2) The why signal is a Wikipedia article, not a curriculum or demand signal; MIT OCW HST.151 Principles of Pharmacology, lecture 1 'Drug-Receptor Interactions', covers it. (3) The IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology database is licensed ODbL; only its text content is CC BY-SA 4.0.
judgeNotes: build 4: The operational model and Gaddum-Schild equations are closed-form, with mass-action binding animated on top; it is honest but mostly evaluates curves rather than simulating, and the optional IUPHAR data is ODbL/CC BY-SA, so share-alike must be honoured if used.

fit-level 4: Mass-action binding, Schild shifts and spare receptors are the real pharmacodynamics model a pharmacology student learns, and the page pairs cleanly with the proposed pharmacokinetics page without overlapping it.

gapEntries.title: Retrieval: how a chatbot looks things up
gapEntries.interaction: Pick one of several questions about a small shelf of documents. Watch the documents split into chunks and embed as points; the question becomes a point too, and the nearest chunks light up and are pasted into the prompt. Change the chunk size and the number of chunks retrieved, or remove the document that holds the answer, and compare a small model's next-token probabilities for the answer with and without the retrieved text (precomputed for every combination).
gapEntries.takeaway: A chatbot that 'searches' does not change its weights: it finds the passages whose embeddings sit closest to the question and puts them into the prompt, so its answer is only as good as what retrieval put there.
gapEntries.needs: A small document set, either public-domain texts (for example NASA or US government pages) or Simple English Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0); embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0), run in the browser or precomputed; next-token probabilities with and without context from a small open model such as SmolLM2-135M-Instruct (Apache 2.0), precomputed.
gapEntries.pitfall: Retrieval does not make answers true: a model can still ignore or misread the retrieved passage, and the nearest chunk by embedding is not always the one that answers the question.
gapEntries.why: Stanford CS224V lists retrieval-augmented generation among its topics (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224v), and Stanford CS25 recorded a lecture on retrieval-augmented language models (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs25/recordings).
gapEntries.overlapWith: embeddings: that page measures nearness between word vectors; this one uses nearness between question and passage vectors to choose what goes into a language model's prompt, and shows the effect on its answer.
gapEntries.needsSource: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0); SmolLM2 (Apache 2.0); documents public domain or CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike must be honoured)
gapEntries.verifyNote: Not a duplicate of embeddings or language-models, and the licences hold up: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and SmolLM2 are Apache 2.0, and Simple English Wikipedia is CC BY-SA 4.0, whose share-alike requirement is noted. Three problems. (1) The interaction says 'Ask a question', which implies free text, but the next-token probabilities are precomputed, so only a fixed set of questions works across the combinations of chunk size, number of chunks and removed document. (2) The 'why' signal is a dev.to blog post, which is weak; Stanford courses teach retrieval-augmented generation (CS224V lists it; CS25 has Douwe Kiela's lecture on retrieval-augmented language models). (3) The page needs nothing from the level-3 transformers page; embeddings and language-models (both level 2) are enough.
judgeNotes: build 4: Chunking and nearest-neighbour retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0) are real and cheap, but the generation side is a precomputed SmolLM2 (Apache 2.0) table over every combination of question, chunk size, k and removed document, so the control grid must stay small; it is honest if labelled as precomputed real model outputs, with CC BY-SA honoured for any Wikipedia text.

fit-level 4: Retrieval into the prompt is central to how deployed chatbots work and fills a gap in the LLM set, with a real mechanism (embedding nearness, then a change in next-token probabilities); the mechanism is simple enough that level 2 or 3 both fit, and level 3 is acceptable given its prerequisites.

gapEntries.title: Microwave ovens & their hot spots
gapEntries.interaction: Switch on a microwave oven seen from above: a wave simulation fills the metal box, and a slab of food warms where the field is strong, shown as a heat map. Stop the turntable to see fixed hot and cold spots, start it to even them out, and lay a chocolate bar across the floor to measure the gap between melted spots against the wavelength.
gapEntries.takeaway: Microwaves reflecting off the metal walls form a standing pattern of strong and weak spots that stays fixed in the box, which is why food heats unevenly and why the turntable moves the food through it.
gapEntries.needs: None: a 2D finite-difference wave (or Helmholtz) solver in a rectangular cavity at 2.45 GHz with a lossy dielectric slab; standard permittivity values for water and food from textbook tables.
gapEntries.pitfall: 2.45 GHz is not a special resonance of water molecules, and microwaves do not cook food from the inside out; they heat the outer few centimetres, and the chocolate spacing is only roughly half a free-space wavelength because the cavity's modes are not a simple standing wave.
gapEntries.why: The chocolate-in-the-microwave speed-of-light experiment is a classic school lesson: https://www.bu.edu/gk12/loren/lesson_microwave.html
gapEntries.overlapWith: waves-interference: that page shows standing waves and interference on strings and in open space; this one applies them in a closed metal box with an absorbing load, where the pattern decides what gets hot.
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound. The prerequisite waves-interference is level 1, the same as the candidate. It does not duplicate waves-interference or wireless-signals: neither shows a closed metal cavity with an absorbing load, a heat map or a turntable. The model is a 2D Helmholtz or FDTD solve on a grid of about 30 by 30 cm at a 12 cm wavelength. That is small enough to compute once, and heating accumulated over the turntable angle can be drawn as a pure function of time. The physics in the pitfall checks out: 2.45 GHz is not a water resonance (water's broad absorption peaks near 20 GHz and above), penetration depth is about 1 to 3 cm, and the chocolate experiment is a standard school lesson (the BU GK-12 URL resolves). Permittivities for water and food are textbook values, so no licence problem. Caveat for the builder: a top-down 2D field is a simplification of a 3D oven's modes, and the page should not claim a quantitatively real oven pattern.
judgeNotes: build 4: A 2D FDTD or Helmholtz solve in a rectangular cavity at 2.45 GHz with a lossy slab is feasible on a modest grid, and rotating the load to time-average the heating is cheap; the real oven is a 3D problem, so the 2D cut must be stated, but the hot-spot spacing comes out honestly.
fit-level 4: An everyday device whose standing-wave hot spots and chocolate-bar measurement apply waves-interference to a closed cavity, making it a distinct and honest level-1 page.

gapEntries.title: Static electricity: why a balloon sticks to the wall
gapEntries.interaction: Rub a balloon on a jumper, one stroke at a time, and count the tiny charges that hop from the jumper to the balloon. Bring the balloon near a wall: the wall's charges lean away or toward it without leaving, and the balloon sticks. Hang two rubbed balloons side by side and they push each other apart.
gapEntries.takeaway: Rubbing moves charges from one thing to another; opposite charges pull and like charges push, and even an uncharged wall is pulled because its charges shift a little toward or away from the balloon.
gapEntries.needs: None: point charges with Coulomb forces; the jumper, balloon and wall are insulators whose charges shift slightly in place, as in PhET's model.
gapEntries.pitfall: Rubbing does not create charge, it only moves it from one thing to the other (the tiny charged bits that move are not the atoms' centres), and the wall the balloon sticks to is not itself charged overall: its charges only shift a little.
gapEntries.why: PhET's 'Balloons and Static Electricity' is one of its most used simulations (CC BY): https://clixplatform.tiss.ac.in/phet/en/simulation/balloons.html
gapEntries.overlapWith: magnets-and-poles: that page is about magnetic poles, which always come in pairs; this one is about electric charges that can be separated and moved by rubbing.
gapEntries.verifyNote: Two small problems. (a) leadsTo lists electromagnetism, which is level 2 in TOPICS.md, but a level-0 page's leadsTo should name level-1 topics only (electric-circuits and atoms-periodic-table are level 1). (b) The pitfall says flatly that rubbing moves 'electrons, not protons'. Protons never move, but what carries the charge when two insulators touch (electrons, ions or nanoscale bits of material) is still debated; see APS Physics https://physics.aps.org/articles/v7/58 and Chemistry World on material transfer. The page must not present electron transfer as settled for a balloon. Everything else holds up: there is no real duplicate (electromagnetism places fixed charges at level 2 and does not show charging by contact or polarization), PhET's sim shows the point-charge model runs fine in a browser, no data is needed, and the takeaway can be seen in the graphic.
judgeNotes: build 4: Coulomb point charges with transfer on rubbing and bound charges that shift slightly in the wall, as in PhET's Balloons and Static Electricity, are a small honest model; the attraction to the wall must come from the computed polarisation forces, not a scripted stick.
fit-level 4: A familiar experience with a countable charge-transfer mechanism and induced polarisation, honest at level 0 and distinct from electric-circuits and magnets-and-poles.

gapEntries.title: How rivers carve mountains: landscape evolution
gapEntries.interaction: Lift a block of land at a steady rate on a grid and let rain run downhill: each cell drains to its steepest neighbour, rivers erode at a rate set by their drainage area and slope (the stream-power law), and hillslopes creep by diffusion. Watch a branching drainage network and ridges emerge until erosion balances uplift; double the uplift rate and the steady-state mountains grow taller and steeper, make the rock harder and the same happens, then switch the uplift off and watch the relief decay.
gapEntries.takeaway: Mountain ranges reach a steady state in which rivers erode them as fast as tectonics lifts them, so how high and steep they stand is set by the uplift rate and the rock, not by their age.
gapEntries.needs: Optional: a real digital elevation model tile for comparison, from SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain). The simulation itself needs no data.
gapEntries.pitfall: The stream-power law is an empirical erosion rule with poorly constrained exponents, not a fundamental law; and steady-state topography means the form persists while rock keeps moving up and being removed, not that nothing happens.
gapEntries.why: Landscape evolution modelling with the stream-power incision model (FastScape) is taught as a core geomorphology method, e.g. the Cologne IRTG course by Jean Braun: https://sfb1211.uni-koeln.de/index.php/74-irtg/events/past-events/141-irtg-rtd-landscape-evolution-modeling-using-the-fastscape-algorithm-software
gapEntries.overlapWith: plate-tectonics builds mountains where plates meet; this page adds the erosion that wears them down and shows the drainage network and steady-state relief that emerge from uplift against river incision.
gapEntries.verifyNote: No existing page covers erosion or drainage networks: plate-tectonics only builds relief. D8 flow routing plus implicit stream-power incision (Braun and Willett 2013) and hillslope diffusion runs at interactive rates on a grid of about 128x128 in the browser. The takeaway matches Whipple and Tucker (1999), where steady-state relief scales with uplift rate and erodibility, and the pitfall correctly says the exponents m and n are poorly constrained. Prerequisites (plate-tectonics, deep-time, calculus) are existing and below level 3. No data is needed; SRTM is public domain.
judgeNotes: build 5: Steepest-descent flow routing, drainage-area accumulation, implicit stream-power incision and hillslope diffusion on a ~128x128 grid run at interactive rates (the standard FastScape-style scheme), and need no data.

fit-level 3: The stream-power plus diffusion landscape model is real and visual, and steady-state relief is a genuine level-3 insight distinct from plate-tectonics, but it is niche, and its rivers-carve-valleys sibling in this batch shares much of the same picture.

gapEntries.title: Cyclic voltammetry: reading a reaction from a current
gapEntries.interaction: Sweep an electrode's potential up and back down and watch the concentration profile of the oxidised and reduced species near the electrode, solved as diffusion on a 1D grid with Butler-Volmer kinetics at the surface, while the current traces the duck-shaped voltammogram. Speed up the scan and the peaks grow with the square root of the scan rate; slow the electron transfer and the two peaks pull apart from about 57 mV toward an irreversible wave; add a follow-up chemical reaction and the return peak shrinks.
gapEntries.takeaway: The current peaks not when the reaction is fastest but when diffusion can no longer bring fresh molecules to the depleted electrode, and the shape and spacing of the peaks reveal how fast electrons transfer.
gapEntries.pitfall: The peak potential is not the standard potential, and the peak separation of about 57/n mV (2.22RT/nF, often misquoted as 59 mV) holds only for a fast, reversible couple at 25 °C; the current falls after the peak because the diffusion layer thickens, not because the bulk solution has run out.
gapEntries.why: Elgrishi et al., 'A Practical Beginner's Guide to Cyclic Voltammetry', J. Chem. Educ. 2018, 95, 197-206, a widely used teaching reference on how scan rate and electron-transfer kinetics shape a voltammogram: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jchemed.7b00361
gapEntries.overlapWith: redox-batteries shows a cell charging and discharging at equilibrium voltages; this page is the measurement technique of electrochemistry, with electrode kinetics and diffusion producing a voltammogram, which nothing on the site models.
gapEntries.verifyNote: The model (1D finite-difference diffusion with Butler-Volmer boundary kinetics and an optional EC follow-up reaction) is a standard teaching simulation and runs at interactive rates. No existing page covers it, the level 3 is honest, and the prerequisites are at or below level 3. But the entry repeats a common error: for a reversible couple the theoretical peak separation is 2.22RT/nF, about 57/n mV at 25 °C; 59 mV is the Nernst slope, often misquoted as the peak separation. Both the interaction and the pitfall must be corrected. The 'why' URL is an R-package vignette on a CRAN mirror rather than a course or demand signal; Elgrishi et al. 2018 (J. Chem. Educ.) is a stronger one.
judgeNotes: build 5: A 1D finite-difference diffusion grid with a Butler-Volmer boundary is the textbook digital simulation of CV, cheap in the browser, and the sqrt(scan rate) and peak-separation results come straight out of it with no data.
fit-level 3: An honest level-3 model (diffusion plus Butler-Volmer) that nothing on the site covers, but it is a lab measurement technique with narrower appeal to visitors than most candidates.

gapEntries.title: Where rain comes from: the water cycle
gapEntries.interaction: A side view of sea, land, hills and sky holds a few thousand water parcels. The reader moves one slider, the sunshine, and watches parcels leave the warm sea as vapour, rise, turn into cloud as they cool over the hills, fall as rain and run back down rivers to the sea. Counters show how much water is in the sea, the air, the clouds and the rivers at each moment.
gapEntries.takeaway: The same water goes round and round: the Sun lifts it from the sea, cooling turns it into cloud and rain, and rivers carry it back, so the total never changes.
gapEntries.needs: none (a parcel model with evaporation rising with temperature and condensation when air cools with height; no external data)
gapEntries.pitfall: Clouds are not water vapour: vapour is invisible, and clouds are tiny liquid drops or ice. And evaporation does not need boiling; puddles dry at everyday temperatures, just faster when it is warm.
gapEntries.why: KS2 Year 4 statutory: identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and link the rate of evaporation to temperature (https://thenational.academy/teachers/programmes/science-primary-ks2/units/introduction-to-states-of-matter-and-changing-states/lessons/evaporation-and-condensation-in-the-water-cycle); also NGSS MS-ESS2-4. The catalogue notes the water cycle is not covered.
gapEntries.overlapWith: cloud-base: that page explains why one cloud forms and why its base is flat; this one follows water all the way round the loop, sea to sky to river, and keeps the total constant.
gapEntries.verifyNote: The catalogue explicitly lists the water cycle as not covered. The proposed cloud-base page explains one cloud, while this page follows the whole loop with conserved counters, so the takeaway (the total never changes) can be read from the counters alone. A parcel model with temperature-dependent evaporation and condensation on cooling runs easily in the browser and needs no external data. The KS2 Year 4 and MS-ESS2-4 signals are real. Level 0 is honest: one slider, no formulas. leadsTo names existing level-1 slugs (states-of-matter, carbon-cycle). The pitfall (clouds are liquid or ice, not vapour; evaporation needs no boiling) is correct. Leaving out evaporation from land and plants is an acceptable simplification for this level.
judgeNotes: build 3: Buildable as a parcel agent model with temperature-dependent evaporation and condensation on cooling with height, but unless the rates follow a real saturation law (Clausius-Clapeyron) and a lapse rate, the model risks becoming a scripted loop dressed as a simulation; the spec should require them.
fit-level 4: A core primary-school subject with a visible loop mechanism and a single sunshine control; it fits level 0 well and is distinct from cloud-base and states-of-matter.

gapEntries.title: How rivers carve valleys
gapEntries.interaction: A sandbox hillside on a grid, like a classroom stream table. The reader tilts it (one control at a time: slope, then how much water) and pours water at the top; the water finds the lowest path, picks up sand where it runs fast and drops it where it slows, cutting a branching valley and building a fan of sand at the bottom.
gapEntries.takeaway: Fast water picks sand up and slow water puts it down, so a steeper slope or more water cuts a deeper valley and builds a bigger fan of sand at the bottom.
gapEntries.needs: none (grid hydraulic-erosion model: water routed downhill, sediment capacity rising with flow speed, erosion and deposition; no external data)
gapEntries.pitfall: Rivers do not dig valleys in one flood or in a single direction downwards; they also drop most of what they carry, and the landscape is as much built by deposition as cut by erosion.
gapEntries.why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1, evidence of weathering and the rate of erosion by water, with slope and water volume as the suggested variables, the classic stream-table investigation (https://thewonderofscience.com/4ess21).
gapEntries.overlapWith: plate-tectonics: that page raises mountains by moving plates; this one wears land down and moves it with running water, which no existing page shows.
gapEntries.verifyNote: A sound level-0 topic with a strong NGSS 4-ESS2-1 stream-table signal, and no existing page shows erosion. Three claims are wrong. (1) A grid hydraulic-erosion model (water routed downhill, transport capacity rising with speed) makes branching channels and fans, but not true meanders: meander growth depends on secondary flow in bends and on bank erosion, which this model leaves out. Promising meanders breaks the rule that the model is real. (2) The interaction builds a fan at the foot of the slope, but the takeaway calls it a delta; a delta forms where a river enters standing water. (3) everyday=true is wrong: a river valley is not an everyday object or household mechanism.
judgeNotes: build 4: Grid hydraulic erosion with flow routing and speed-dependent sediment capacity is a well-known, fast browser algorithm that produces channels and a fan; it is honest at level 0, though it shares its engine with landscape-evolution.

fit-level 3: The stream-table erosion and deposition mechanism is honest at level 0 and new to the site, but it overlaps visually with landscape-evolution in this batch, so only one of the two may be worth keeping.

gapEntries.title: Lightning: how a bolt finds the ground
gapEntries.interaction: Charge a thundercloud above a landscape and watch a stepped leader grow down from it in jagged jumps, each step chosen at random but more likely where the electric field is strongest. Add a tree, a tower or a lightning rod: an upward streamer rises to meet the leader, the channel connects and the bright return stroke runs from the ground up. Raise or lower the cloud's charge and compare how often the tall object is the one that gets hit.
gapEntries.takeaway: Lightning branches because it grows step by step toward wherever the electric field is strongest, and tall pointed objects make the field strong enough near them to launch a streamer that often, but not always, catches the leader.
gapEntries.needs: None: the dielectric breakdown model (Niemeyer, Pietronero and Wiesmann 1984), which solves the Laplace equation on a grid and grows the channel with probability proportional to a power of the local field; stroke timings and currents from NOAA/NWS public-domain material.
gapEntries.pitfall: The bright flash does not travel down from the cloud: the visible return stroke goes up the channel from the ground; and lightning can strike the same place twice. The model's branching exponent is fitted, not derived, and a 2D grid gives flatter branching than real 3D bolts.
gapEntries.why: The US National Weather Service explains the stepped leader and return stroke for the public: https://weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-negative-charged-flash
gapEntries.overlapWith: atmosphere-weather: that page covers winds, fronts and storms at the scale of the globe; this one zooms into one discharge and models how its path grows and where it lands.
gapEntries.needsSource: none (computed model; facts from NOAA/NWS, US public domain)
gapEntries.verifyNote: The dielectric breakdown model (Niemeyer, Pietronero and Wiesmann 1984) is a real, cheap grid model: relax the Laplace equation, then grow the channel with probability proportional to a power of the local field. It runs at interactive rates on a grid of about 100x100. An upward streamer from a tall object is a small, documented extension. The NWS page exists and confirms the stepped leader in roughly 50 m steps, the upward streamer connecting within about 50 m of the ground, and the return stroke moving up the channel. So the pitfall is correct, and it honestly states that the branching exponent is fitted and that a 2D grid flattens the branching. The page overlaps neither atmosphere-weather (global circulation) nor electromagnetism (field lines of point charges). Level 1 with electric-circuits as prerequisite is acceptable, since electric fields from static charge are GCSE content. The takeaway (branching toward strong field, tall objects often but not always hit) can be seen in the graphic.
judgeNotes: build 4: The Niemeyer-Pietronero-Wiesmann dielectric breakdown model, a grid Laplace relaxation with field-weighted growth, runs interactively on roughly 100x100 grids with incremental solves, and tall-object strike statistics can be computed by repeated runs; the facts come from NOAA/NWS public-domain material.

fit-level 3: A stepped-leader growth model on a field grid is a real mechanism distinct from atmosphere-weather, but it relies on electric fields that the site teaches at level 2 (electromagnetism), and its fitted branching makes it less crisp at level 1.
